### 3. Nikon Z8

The [Nikon Z8](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1765622-REG/nikon_z8_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) can do almost everything that the Nikon Z9 can, not to mention in a much smaller package that costs about $1500 less than the Z9. The lighter weight is a huge benefit for a lot of photographers, and some may prefer the Z8 over the Z9 simply for that reason. That said, the smaller body can overheat a little more easily, especially when shooting 8K video, and it’s missing a few of the more advanced connectivity features of the Z9 (like a built-in GPS).

[![Image 8: Nikon Z8](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2023/05/Nikon-Z8.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Nikon-Z8.jpg)

Nikon’s Z8: The mirrorless successor of the D850, and then some

Like the Z9, the Nikon Z8 does not have a mechanical shutter. Instead, its stacked sensor and electronic-only shutter is fast enough for any purpose. It also has an amazing autofocus system and access to Nikon’s unique array of wildlife lenses. For wildlife photographers, the Z8 is an extraordinary camera.

I recommend the Nikon Z8 over the Z9 for most people who don’t need the built-in vertical grip, or who want something lighter than the Z9. For something like landscape photography where you are hiking a great distance, it’s definitely the camera to choose between the two.

It’s also worth mentioning that the Nikon Z8 won first place in our poll of [Nikon’s greatest camera of all time](https://photographylife.com/best-nikon-camera-all-time)!

### 4. Canon EOS R5 Mark II

It feels criminal to rank the Canon R5 Mark II outside of the top three, but that’s just a testament to how impressive cameras are today. The EOS R5 II is a high-resolution, high-speed beast that’s equally capable of landscape photography and sports/wildlife. In that sense, it’s pretty similar to the three cameras above.

[![Image 10: Canon EOS R5 Body Only](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/07/Canon-EOS-R5-Body-Only.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Canon-EOS-R5-Body-Only.jpg)

The Canon EOS R5 II has a 45-megapixel sensor and can shoot a whopping 30 FPS. It has an excellent autofocus system, and like the three cameras above, it can also shoot 8K video – in this case at a highly impressive 60p. Canon found a way to push a ton of data through the EOS R5’s pipeline, and it makes this camera excellent for action photography and video in addition to its high quality for landscapes.

As you would expect, all of this comes at a high price: the EOS R5 II costs $4400 body only. ([Check the price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1840289-REG/canon_6536c002_eos_r5_mark_ii.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), though; it goes on sale pretty often.) If you can’t find a good deal on the EOS R5 Mark II, the good news is that you can get the previous generation Canon EOS R5 for a more reasonable price [around $3300](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1547009-REG/canon_eos_r5_mirrorless_digital.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), and we’ve even seen it on sale as low as $2600. Compared to the “Mark II,” the original EOS R5 is surprisingly similar – a tad slower, but still blazing fast, and it has the same 45-megapixel sensor. If I were including older generation cameras in this list, I could easily rank the original EOS R5 right below the Mark II.

### 5. Sony A7r V

Almost reaching the lofty heights of the Sony A1 II, yet more than $2500 cheaper, is the Sony A7r V. It sells for $4200 ([check price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1731389-REG/sony_alpha_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1201601/SID/DFF)) and has an even higher-resolution 61-megapixel sensor.

The A7r V still manages to shoot at 10 FPS despite the high-res sensor, and it has a huge buffer of 583 images. For a lot of photographers who are considering the Nikon Z9 or Sony A1 II, the A7R V will actually make more sense. It’s an excellent camera for landscape photography because of the high-res sensor, and at 10 FPS, it’s still great for photographing wildlife, too. It doesn’t quite reach the maximum specifications of either the Z9 or A1, but for most applications, it will do just as well as either of those cameras.

### 6. Canon EOS R1 and EOS R3

If you want a more specialized camera for sports and wildlife photography, it’s hard to beat the Canon EOS R1, or its little brother the R3. Unlike the previous cameras on this list, the EOS R1 and EOS R3 don’t have a 40+ megapixel sensor; instead, they’re “only” 24 megapixels. But these two cameras can shoot more than 30 FPS with a functionally unlimited buffer. They also have Canon’s unique “eye-sensing autofocus” that begins focusing at the spot _you look at in the composition_. It’s a seriously cool feature.

[![Image 14: Canon EOS R3 Front View](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2021/04/Canon-EOS-R3-Front-View.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Canon-EOS-R3-Front-View.jpg)

I paired the two cameras into one entry on this list because they’re surprisingly similar. The main benefits of the EOS R1 are 40 FPS rather than 30 FPS, and a pre-release burst mode. Given that the prices are $6800 and $5400 respectively, I frankly think that a lot of photographers should go with the EOS R3 instead. But if you find pre-release RAW to be worth the extra cash, then of course the flagship EOS R1 has the advantage.

For any fast-paced genres of photography, you’ll want to take a long look at these two cameras. If you don’t need the high-res sensors of the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Sony A7r V, or Canon EOS R5 II, it equals or beats all of them in performance and gives you smaller, more manageable files.

### 7. Sony A7 V

It’s crazy that I haven’t gotten to talk about the Sony A7 V yet – one of the best all-around mirrorless cameras that you can get today, and a great deal, too.

This $2900 camera ([check price](https://bhpho.to/49NKSP6)) has a 33-megapixel sensor, which is a sweet spot for both landscape and wildlife photography. At 30 FPS blackout-free shooting, and borrowing its autofocus system from the Sony A1, it’s an incredible choice for fast-moving action.

### 8. Sony A9 III

The Sony A9 III presents entirely new possibilities with its 24-megapixel global shutter. This single innovation completely eliminates rolling shutter and allows flash photography to work at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync.

Due to its new shutter technology, it has an incredible 1/80,000 minimum shutter speed and can shoot at 120fps. It seems very unlikely that anything in the normal world will be too fast for this camera.

[At $6000](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1794764-REG/sony_ilce_9m3_a9_iii_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), the Sony A9 III is arguably overpriced, and many of the other cameras here will beat it for other applications – i.e., anything other than sports. This is definitely a highly specialized camera. Still, if you’re aching to use a global shutter, there’s no other camera on this list _but_ the Sony A9III.

### 9. Canon EOS R6 Mark III

Alongside the Sony A7 V, one of the best mirrorless cameras today in terms of price-vs-features is the Canon EOS R6 Mark III. This camera is a replacement for the prior generation EOS R6 Mark II that also remains an excellent choice.

The EOS R6 Mark III and even the Mark II are practically as good as the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Canon R5 II, and other top cameras where autofocus is concerned. One of the best values on this entire list is the Nikon Z5 II. Despite being a full-frame camera with plenty of advanced features, including an autofocus system that practically matches that of the Nikon Z8 and Z9, I’ve seen it go as low as $1600 new ([check current sales](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1889823-REG/nikon_1680_z5_ii_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400)).

It’s pretty much a “Z6 III lite” and only loses at the margins: 15 FPS rather than 20, a 12-second buffer rather than unlimited, no 6K video, and a less advanced viewfinder. If you’re on a budget, it’s hard to beat the Nikon Z5 II – although I will point out that the previous generation Z5 is about the cheapest possible full-frame mirrorless camera, especially if bought used, and it’s a solid camera if you don’t need a top-notch AF system.

### 15. Panasonic S5 II

One area where Panasonic had been lagging behind the best mirrorless cameras from Nikon, Canon, and Sony was autofocus performance (at least in Panasonic’s full-frame cameras). The Panasonic S5 II fixes this by introducing the company’s phase-detect AF.

[![Image 28: Panasonic S5 II](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Panasonic-S5-II.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Panasonic-S5-II.jpg)

Although the S5 II has a 24-megapixel sensor, don’t let that fool you if you’re a landscape photographer. Like some of the Sony and Fuji cameras on this list, the Panasonic S5 II has a high-resolution pixel-shift mode that quadruples a photo’s resolution to 96 megapixels! This only works if the subject is staying still, but I found that it produces fairly natural results in previous Panasonic mirrorless cameras, like the Panasonic S1R (see [our review](https://photographylife.com/reviews/panasonic-s1r)).

The Panasonic S5 II also has some very good video features, capturing up to 6K video internally. It even has a dedicated cooling fan to allow the camera to keep filming for long stretches without overheating. Add that to the 200-image RAW buffer, the 30 FPS shooting, and the $2000 price, and you have a very versatile mirrorless camera indeed.

### 16. Nikon Z7 II

If you want a high-resolution camera that’s excellent for landscape photography, you should look closely at the 45 megapixel, $3000 [Nikon Z7 II](https://photographylife.com/reviews/nikon-z7-ii).

[![Image 30: Nikon Z7 II](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/10/Nikon-Z7-II.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Nikon-Z7-II.jpg)

Even though the Nikon Z7 II isn’t as fast as some other mirrorless cameras – including most of Nikon’s other cameras – it would be one of my top few choices on the market for landscape photography. An unsung feature of the Nikon Z7 II is the base ISO of 64, giving it dynamic range that rivals even medium format! Not to mention that the Z lenses are some of the sharpest lenses of all time, making it an ideal system to capture a lot of detail without weighing very much.

When the Nikon Z7 II was released, it got some bad press for the autofocus system’s wildlife photography capabilities. Of course, it’s all relative: I found that even the previous generation Z7 was [perfectly fine for fast wildlife](https://photographylife.com/bad-autofocus-wildlife-photography) once you get the hang of it. But it’s true that you’d be better served with something like the Canon EOS R5 II, Sony A7r V, or Nikon Z8 if wildlife photography is a priority for you.

[![Image 31: Nikon Z7 II Image Samples #40](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-40.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-40.jpg)

NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S @ 24mm, ISO 64, 2.5 seconds, f/11.0

### 17. Fujifilm X-T5

I’m a big fan of Fuji’s mirrorless cameras, and the X-T5 has some of the company’s best features so far.

[![Image 32: Fuji X-T4](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/08/Fuji-X-T4.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Fuji-X-T4.jpg)

With its 40-megapixel X-Trans sensor capable of producing excellent image quality, in-body image stabilization, a fast X-Processor 4 with Quad CPU that is capable of pushing up 6K video, F-Log gamma for extended dynamic range when shooting video, long battery life, an insanely fast and accurate autofocus system, and a bright 3.69 million dot EVF, the Fuji X-T3 is an impressive stills and video camera. It even shoots 15 FPS (20 FPS if you don’t mind a 1.3x crop), making it a good camera for sports and wildlife, too.

While it is an exceptionally good camera in many ways, it is still an APS-C sensor camera, so it doesn’t do as well at high ISOs or shallow depth of field as the other cameras on this list. It’s also more expensive than most APS-C cameras at $1700 ([check price and availability](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1731281-REG/fujifilm_16782301_x_t5_mirrorless_camera_black.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1202904/SID/DFF)). You may want to consider the prior generation X-T4, too, which [I’ve seen go on sale](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1548388-REG/fujifilm_16652855_x_t4_mirrorless_digital_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) now that the X-T5 is out.

[![Image 33: Fuji X-T3 Image Sample (2)](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Fuji-X-T3-Image-Sample-2.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Fuji-X-T3-Image-Sample-2.jpg)

Captured with Fuji X-T4 + XF 23mmF2 R WR @ 23mm, ISO 160, 0.6 sec, f/5.6

### 18. Fujifilm X-H2S

If you want speed in a crop-sensor camera, the [Fuji X-H2S](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1708265-REG/fujifilm_16756924_x_h2s_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) is for you. It has a stacked 26MP sensor, which is plenty of resolution for most situations. And it’s _fast_.

[![Image 34: H2s](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2022/05/H2s.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/H2s.jpg)

Thanks to the camera’s stacked BSI sensor, it can shoot RAW photos at 40 FPS. At that frame rate, your buffer is still a very reasonable 140 images. Drop the burst down to 15 FPS, and you’ll get a 1000-image buffer. So, to say that this camera is good for fast action is an understatement.

The X-H2S also has some very impressive video features with excellent-quality footage – not only with 4K120 but also with 6K 30p. Between this camera and the X-T5 above, I consider the X-T5 more versatile because of its higher-resolution sensor, but the X-H2S isn’t far behind.

### 19. Canon EOS R7

Another fast, APS-C camera that has been turning a lot of heads is the Canon EOS R7. [At $1500](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1707911-REG/canon_eos_r7_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1178028/SID/DFF), it’s about $1000 less expensive than the Fuji X-H2S while nipping at its heels in terms of features.

![Image 35: Canon EOS R7 Front](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2022/05/Canon-EOS-R7-Front.jpg/w=650)

Those features begin with a 32.5-megapixel sensor, which is high for an APS-C camera. The EOS R7 has a 30 FPS burst, 4K 60p filming, in-body image stabilization, and a great autofocus system. It also has one of my favorite features, a pre-release burst mode that allows you to record photos up to 1/2 second before you’ve fully pressed the shutter button. This is great for unpredictable wildlife photography.

One potential issue is that the buffer is not as big as that of the Fuji X-H2S. The Canon EOS R7 gives you 93 shots at 30 FPS and 187 shots at 15 FPS (assuming that you’re using lossless compressed CRAW). These figures are not low, but not best-in-class either. Even so,the EOS R7 would be one of my first choices for sports and wildlife photography on a budget today.

### 20. Nikon Z50 II

Nikon’s attempt at a high-speed APS-C camera is the Z50 II, and it’s a very good camera in many ways. The autofocus system is borrowed from the flagship Nikon Z9, so it’s a highly capable camera for sports and wildlife photography.

![Image 36: Nikon Z50 II_01](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_01.jpg/w=650)

The main downside of this camera is the 20 megapixel resolution – tied for the lowest on this list. 20 megapixels is still plenty for most prints, but it doesn’t leave as much room for cropping, and in today’s world, a lot of people would prefer something over 30 MP just in case they’re making large prints.

Still, the price is good ([around $1000](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1860621-REG/nikon_1784_z50_ii_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400)) and the features are very impressive. This camera could be an excellent choice depending on your priorities.

[![Image 37: Nikon Z50 II_Sample Images_DSC_0263](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_Sample-Images_DSC_0263.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_Sample-Images_DSC_0263.jpg)

NIKON Z50_2 + NIKKOR Z 180-600mm f/5.6-6.3 VR @ 600mm, ISO 25600, 1/250, f/6.3

### 21. Canon EOS R8

This 24-megapixel, full-frame mirrorless camera is aimed at a budget-conscious audience (at least among full-frame cameras) with a price of $1500. It sometimes goes on sale for less; [check the current price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1748813-REG/canon_eos_r8_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1219667/SID/DFF)).

![Image 38: Canon EOS R8 Official Product Photo](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2023/02/Canon-EOS-R8-Official-Product-Photo.jpg/w=650)

Benefits of the EOS R8 include 40 FPS shooting (electronic shutter) and Canon’s pre-release shutter mode. A drawback of this camera is that it doesn’t have in-body image stabilization, and it has just a single SD card slot. Still, these compromises are what allowed Canon to keep the price of the EOS R8 relatively low. It’s still a great camera with impressive bang for your buck.

### 22. OM System OM-1

In the realm of micro four thirds, the [OM System OM-1](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1688415-REG/om_system_v210010bu000_om_1_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) is an amazing camera for sports photography and wildlife photography. It also has some of the most modern features of any camera on this list.

![Image 39: OM1_OM_SYSTEM](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/OM1_OM_SYSTEM.png/w=9999)

Not only does it have a stacked 20MP sensor, it has an insane 120fps burst capability and advanced subject recognition modes for almost every situation.If you don’t want to carry around a massive full-frame camera, and you want access to some very compact, yet high-quality lenses, the OM-1 is worth considering.

The downside, of course, is the smaller sensor size. Obviously Micro Four Thirds has a dedicated audience of photographers, and for something like wildlife or macro photography, it’s may not be a hinderance at all. But bigger sensors allow you to shoot in low-light conditions more easily, and they give you more flexibility in your depth of field. To match a full-frame camera with an 85mm f/1.2 lens, for example, you would need a (nonexistent) 42mm f/0.6 on Micro Four Thirds.

Whether that matters to you or not depends on your style of photography. If you’re not the type to need maximum dynamic range, high ISO performance, or shallow depth of field, the OM-1 can beat almost any other camera on this list in features.The fact that such an amazing camera is low on our list is not a negative for the OM-1, but rather a statement about how good today’s mirrorless cameras are.

### Conclusion

I hope this article helped you get a sense of where things stand as of 2026, from someone who has used literally dozens of mirrorless cameras during my time reviewing them on Photography Life. # The Best Mirrorless Cameras of 2026, Ranked

By [Nasim Mansurov](https://photographylife.com/author/megaz)97 Comments  
Last Updated On April 8, 2026

![Image 1: Best Cameras Illustration](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/11/Best-Cameras-Illustration.png/w=9999)

Thanks to the vast number of mirrorless cameras we have available today, it can be very difficult to choose the right one. That’s especially true when you’re trying to balance features against budget constraints. Which mirrorless camera actually walks that tightrope the best?

[![Image 2: Nikon Z7 II Image Samples #31](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-31.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-31.jpg)

NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 20mm f/1.8 S @ 20mm, ISO 64, 1.3 seconds, f/5.6  
Copyright © Nasim Mansurov

The answer is going to be different for every photographer, but I’ve been lucky enough to test literally dozens of mirrorless cameras over the years for our many [camera reviews](https://photographylife.com/camera-reviews) at Photography Life, including some mirrorless cameras which we haven’t even reviewed yet. So, I figured that today was a good time to do a list of the best mirrorless cameras on the market today, as of 2026.

Make sure to check out our [Mirrorless vs DSLR](https://photographylife.com/mirrorless-vs-dslr) guide, and our [Best DSLR Cameras](https://photographylife.com/best-dslr-camera) list if you want more information, too.

![Image 3: An illustration showing top mirrorless cameras of 2020](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Best-Mirrorless-Cameras.jpg/w=9999)

### Considerations for the “Best” Mirrorless Camera

It’s very hard to rank cameras from best to worst, not least because every camera out there is the best for _someone_. The camera that works for my photography may be a bad choice for you, and vice versa.

That’s my disclosure for this article: read the descriptions before getting mad about my rankings! Heck, the mirrorless camera that I personally use isn’t even in the top 5. No hard feelings if your favorite camera isn’t number one.

I tried to prioritize cameras that are good at almost anything you could throw at them: high-speed, high-resolution beasts with great autofocus systems, large buffers, and modern features. Such a thing is impossible, of course, but that’s what I aimed for. Also,_I excluded older generation cameras from this list, but I still discussed them where relevant_. That’s because the best-of-the-best is simply something that involves newer cameras most of the time. However, older cameras can be excellent choices too, especially for the money.

Speaking of money, in the end, I only really took price into account as a tie-breaker when ranking these cameras. I figure that you can set your budget ahead of time, then look for the highest-ranked cameras on this list that fall within your budget.

Without further ado, here is my list of the top mirrorless cameras as of 2026:

### 1. Nikon Z9

[![Image 4: Nikon Z9](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2022/07/Nikon-Z9.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Nikon-Z9.jpg)

The Nikon Z9 is a workhorse no matter what subject you throw at it. This camera is [Nikon’s best wildlife photography camera](https://photographylife.com/best-nikon-camera-wildlife-photography)_and_[Nikon’s second best landscape photography camera](https://photographylife.com/best-nikon-camera-landscape-photography). It has a 45-megapixel sensor, yet shoots 20 FPS bursts with a practically unlimited buffer (1000+ shots). And even though it’s expensive at $5900 ([check price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1629829-REG/nikon_z_9_mirrorless_digital.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400)), that’s still a remarkable value for what you get. Plus, Nikon has improved it significantly over the years to the point that today’s Z9 is practically a second-generation camera. Indeed, it is these extensive updates that led me to rank it #1 — the addition of so many new features over time (which we detailed [here](https://photographylife.com/nikon-z9-firmware-5-30)) has meant this camera constantly kept up with the cutting edge over the years.

Compared to DSLRs like the Nikon D6, the Z9 is more advanced in almost every way, yet less expensive. The only downside for some photographers is that the Z9’s large size and weight make it impractical for long hikes or full days of traveling. And, of course, $5500 is still expensive. If you’re on a budget, it would make sense to get a less expensive camera and put your money toward lenses instead.

### 2. Sony A1 II

The Sony A1 II has extraordinary specifications, competing directly with the Nikon Z9 and in some cases exceeding it. The A1 can shoot 50 megapixel images at 30 frames per second, which is out of this world. It has an amazing autofocus system, too, making for great sports and action photography – alongside the obvious landscape photography applications.

Between the Sony A1 II and the Nikon Z9, it was very hard to pick which one deserved to be ranked higher. A lot of it comes down to whether you prefer the large form factor of a camera with a built-in grip like the Z9, or the portability of the Sony A1 II. In terms of features, the biggest benefit of the Sony A1 II is that it has a RAW pre-capture burst, whereas the Nikon Z9’s pre-capture burst is JPEG-only.

![Image 6: Sony a1 II](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Sony-a1-II.jpg/w=650)

That said, the Sony A1 II is a seriously expensive camera at $7000 ([check price](https://bhpho.to/4qwfyLX)). You may consider going with the previous generation Sony A1 to save a little money, since it’s about $6200 ([check price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1619483-REG/sony_ilce_1_b_alpha_a1_mirrorless_digital.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400)). The two cameras are quite similar, with the A1 II featuring newer autofocus algorithms, although the A1 is hardly a slouch where autofocus is concerned. The previous A1 does not have pre-capture burst, however.

Although the A1 and A1 II are excellent for sports and wildlife photography – and that’s what they’re mainly geared for capturing – I find them to be excellent landscape photography cameras as well. The combination of light weight, high resolution, and excellent lenses is hard to beat.

### 3. Nikon Z8

The [Nikon Z8](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1765622-REG/nikon_z8_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) can do almost everything that the Nikon Z9 can, not to mention in a much smaller package that costs about $1500 less than the Z9. The lighter weight is a huge benefit for a lot of photographers, and some may prefer the Z8 over the Z9 simply for that reason. That said, the smaller body can overheat a little more easily, especially when shooting 8K video, and it’s missing a few of the more advanced connectivity features of the Z9 (like a built-in GPS).

[![Image 8: Nikon Z8](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2023/05/Nikon-Z8.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/Nikon-Z8.jpg)

Like the Z9, the Nikon Z8 does not have a mechanical shutter. Instead, its stacked sensor and electronic-only shutter is fast enough for any purpose. It also has an amazing autofocus system and access to Nikon’s unique array of wildlife lenses. For wildlife photographers, the Z8 is an extraordinary camera.

I recommend the Nikon Z8 over the Z9 for most people who don’t need the built-in vertical grip, or who want something lighter than the Z9. For something like landscape photography where you are hiking a great distance, it’s definitely the camera to choose between the two.

It’s also worth mentioning that the Nikon Z8 won first place in our poll of [Nikon’s greatest camera of all time](https://photographylife.com/best-nikon-camera-all-time)!

### 4. Canon EOS R5 Mark II

It feels criminal to rank the Canon R5 Mark II outside of the top three, but that’s just a testament to how impressive cameras are today. The EOS R5 II is a high-resolution, high-speed beast that’s equally capable of landscape photography and sports/wildlife. In that sense, it’s pretty similar to the three cameras above.

[![Image 10: Canon EOS R5 Body Only](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/07/Canon-EOS-R5-Body-Only.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Canon-EOS-R5-Body-Only.jpg)

The Canon EOS R5 II has a 45-megapixel sensor and can shoot a whopping 30 FPS. It has an excellent autofocus system, and like the three cameras above, it can also shoot 8K video – in this case at a highly impressive 60p. Canon found a way to push a ton of data through the EOS R5’s pipeline, and it makes this camera excellent for action photography and video in addition to its high quality for landscapes.

As you would expect, all of this comes at a high price: the EOS R5 II costs $4400 body only. If you can’t find a good deal on the EOS R5 Mark II, the good news is that you can get the previous generation Canon EOS R5 for a more reasonable price [around $3300](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1547009-REG/canon_eos_r5_mirrorless_digital.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), and we’ve even seen it on sale as low as $2600. Compared to the “Mark II,” the original EOS R5 is surprisingly similar – a tad slower, but still blazing fast, and it has the same 45-megapixel sensor. If I were including older generation cameras in this list, I could easily rank the original EOS R5 right below the Mark II.

### 5. Sony A7r V

Almost reaching the lofty heights of the Sony A1 II, yet more than $2500 cheaper, is the Sony A7r V. It sells for $4200 ([check price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1731389-REG/sony_alpha_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1201601/SID/DFF)) and has an even higher-resolution 61-megapixel sensor.

The A7r V still manages to shoot at 10 FPS despite the high-res sensor, and it has a huge buffer of 583 images. And the autofocus system is incredible: It uses Sony’s newest artificial intelligence, subject-recognition algorithms. Cutting through the buzzwords, this means the A7r V can recognize subjects like birds and people even when they face away from the camera or have an unusual pose.

For a lot of photographers who are considering the Nikon Z9 or Sony A1 II, the A7R V will actually make more sense. It’s an excellent camera for landscape photography because of the high-res sensor, and at 10 FPS, it’s still great for photographing wildlife, too. It doesn’t quite reach the maximum specifications of either the Z9 or A1, but for most applications, it will do just as well as either of those cameras.

### 6. Canon EOS R1 and EOS R3

If you want a more specialized camera for sports and wildlife photography, it’s hard to beat the Canon EOS R1, or its little brother the R3. Unlike the previous cameras on this list, the EOS R1 and EOS R3 don’t have a 40+ megapixel sensor; instead, they’re “only” 24 megapixels. But these two cameras can shoot more than 30 FPS with a functionally unlimited buffer. They also have Canon’s unique “eye-sensing autofocus” that begins focusing at the spot _you look at in the composition_. It’s a seriously cool feature.

[![Image 14: Canon EOS R3 Front View](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2021/04/Canon-EOS-R3-Front-View.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Canon-EOS-R3-Front-View.jpg)

I paired the two cameras into one entry on this list because they’re surprisingly similar. The main benefits of the EOS R1 are 40 FPS rather than 30 FPS, and a pre-release burst mode. Given that the prices are $6800 and $5400 respectively, I frankly think that a lot of photographers should go with the EOS R3 instead. But if you find pre-release RAW to be worth the extra cash, then of course the flagship EOS R1 has the advantage.

For any fast-paced genres of photography, you’ll want to take a long look at these two cameras. If you don’t need the high-res sensors of the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Sony A7r V, or Canon EOS R5 II, it equals or beats all of them in performance and gives you smaller, more manageable files.

It’s crazy that I haven’t gotten to talk about the Sony A7 V yet – one of the best all-around mirrorless cameras that you can get today, and a great deal, too.

This $2900 camera ([check price](https://bhpho.to/49NKSP6)) has a 33-megapixel sensor, which is a sweet spot for both landscape and wildlife photography. At 30 FPS blackout-free shooting, and borrowing its autofocus system from the Sony A1, it’s an incredible choice for fast-moving action.

### 8. Sony A9 III

The Sony A9 III presents entirely new possibilities with its 24-megapixel global shutter. This single innovation completely eliminates rolling shutter and allows flash photography to work at all shutter speeds without high-speed sync.

Due to its new shutter technology, it has an incredible 1/80,000 minimum shutter speed and can shoot at 120fps. It seems very unlikely that anything in the normal world will be too fast for this camera.

[At $6000](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1794764-REG/sony_ilce_9m3_a9_iii_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), the Sony A9 III is arguably overpriced, and many of the other cameras here will beat it for other applications – i.e., anything other than sports. This is definitely a highly specialized camera. Still, if you’re aching to use a global shutter, there’s no other camera on this list _but_ the Sony A9III.

### 9. Canon EOS R6 Mark III

Alongside the Sony A7 V, one of the best mirrorless cameras today in terms of price-vs-features is the Canon EOS R6 Mark III. This camera is a replacement for the prior generation EOS R6 Mark II that also remains an excellent choice.

The EOS R6 III has a 32.5-megapixel sensor (compared to 24 megapixels on the previous R6 II).It shoots up to 40 FPS stills, has dual memory card slots, and uses Canon’s superb dual-pixel mirrorless autofocus system. Unlike the previous generation – and unlike most of the other cameras on this list – it’s capable of shooting 7K RAW video.

It does all this at [a starting price of $2800](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1928858-REG/canon_eos_r6_mark_iii.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400). The EOS R6 Mark III and even the Mark II are practically as good as the Nikon Z9, Sony A1 II, Canon R5 II, and other top cameras where autofocus is concerned. Well done to Canon for putting such a good autofocus system on a less expensive camera. That said, if you’re mainly interested in landscape or studio photography and don’t need so many action photography features, you’d probably happier with one of the other cameras on this list.

One of the best values on this entire list is the Nikon Z5 II. The Nikon Zf is a retro-themed mirrorless camera that pretty much matches the Nikon Z5 II in feature set. The main difference is the design of the camera (and a slightly higher price for the Zf). It’s hard to deny that this is a beautiful camera:

![Image 27: Nikon-Zf-Official-Product-Photo-1](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2023/09/Nikon-Zf-Official-Product-Photo-1.jpg/w=650)

Between the Zf and the Z5 II, the main differences are slightly better battery life on the Zf and slightly better video features on the Z5 II. The [price of the Zf is $2200](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1788062-REG/nikon_1761_zf_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400), though – $350 higher than that of the Z5 II, at least when it’s not on sale. It’s probably a camera that you buy more for the ergonomics and beautiful design, while you’d buy the Z5 II if those things are less important than the price. But you can see more at our [Zf vs Z5 II comparison](https://photographylife.com/comparison/nikon-zf-vs-nikon-z5-ii) to figure out if any of the small differences matter to you.

### 15. Panasonic S5 II

One area where Panasonic had been lagging behind the best mirrorless cameras from Nikon, Canon, and Sony was autofocus performance (at least in Panasonic’s full-frame cameras). The Panasonic S5 II fixes this by introducing the company’s phase-detect AF.

[![Image 28: Panasonic S5 II](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Panasonic-S5-II.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Panasonic-S5-II.jpg)

Although the S5 II has a 24-megapixel sensor, don’t let that fool you if you’re a landscape photographer. Like some of the Sony and Fuji cameras on this list, the Panasonic S5 II has a high-resolution pixel-shift mode that quadruples a photo’s resolution to 96 megapixels! This only works if the subject is staying still, but I found that it produces fairly natural results in previous Panasonic mirrorless cameras, like the Panasonic S1R (see [our review](https://photographylife.com/reviews/panasonic-s1r)).

The Panasonic S5 II also has some very good video features, capturing up to 6K video internally. It even has a dedicated cooling fan to allow the camera to keep filming for long stretches without overheating. Add that to the 200-image RAW buffer, the 30 FPS shooting, and the $2000 price, and you have a very versatile mirrorless camera indeed.

[![Image 29: Hong Kong Blue Hour Taken with Panasonic S1R](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2019/10/Hong-Kong-Blue-Hour-Taken-with-Panasonic-S1R.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/Hong-Kong-Blue-Hour-Taken-with-Panasonic-S1R.jpg)

DC-S1R + LUMIX S 24-105/F4 @ 105mm, ISO 200, 1/1, f/5.0

### 16. Nikon Z7 II

If you want a high-resolution camera that’s excellent for landscape photography, you should look closely at the 45 megapixel, $3000 [Nikon Z7 II](https://photographylife.com/reviews/nikon-z7-ii).

[![Image 30: Nikon Z7 II](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/10/Nikon-Z7-II.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Nikon-Z7-II.jpg)

Even though the Nikon Z7 II isn’t as fast as some other mirrorless cameras – including most of Nikon’s other cameras – it would be one of my top few choices on the market for landscape photography. An unsung feature of the Nikon Z7 II is the base ISO of 64, giving it dynamic range that rivals even medium format! Not to mention that the Z lenses are some of the sharpest lenses of all time, making it an ideal system to capture a lot of detail without weighing very much.

When the Nikon Z7 II was released, it got some bad press for the autofocus system’s wildlife photography capabilities. Of course, it’s all relative: I found that even the previous generation Z7 was [perfectly fine for fast wildlife](https://photographylife.com/bad-autofocus-wildlife-photography) once you get the hang of it. But it’s true that you’d be better served with something like the Canon EOS R5 II, Sony A7r V, or Nikon Z8 if wildlife photography is a priority for you.

[![Image 31: Nikon Z7 II Image Samples #40](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-40.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/04/Nikon-Z7-II-Image-Samples-40.jpg)

NIKON Z 7 II + NIKKOR Z 14-24mm f/2.8 S @ 24mm, ISO 64, 2.5 seconds, f/11.0

### 17. Fujifilm X-T5

I’m a big fan of Fuji’s mirrorless cameras, and the X-T5 has some of the company’s best features so far.

[![Image 32: Fuji X-T4](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2020/08/Fuji-X-T4.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Fuji-X-T4.jpg)

With its 40-megapixel X-Trans sensor capable of producing excellent image quality, in-body image stabilization, a fast X-Processor 4 with Quad CPU that is capable of pushing up 6K video, F-Log gamma for extended dynamic range when shooting video, long battery life, an insanely fast and accurate autofocus system, and a bright 3.69 million dot EVF, the Fuji X-T3 is an impressive stills and video camera. It even shoots 15 FPS (20 FPS if you don’t mind a 1.3x crop), making it a good camera for sports and wildlife, too.

While it is an exceptionally good camera in many ways, it is still an APS-C sensor camera, so it doesn’t do as well at high ISOs or shallow depth of field as the other cameras on this list. It’s also more expensive than most APS-C cameras at $1700 ([check price and availability](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1731281-REG/fujifilm_16782301_x_t5_mirrorless_camera_black.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1202904/SID/DFF)). You may want to consider the prior generation X-T4, too, which [I’ve seen go on sale](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1548388-REG/fujifilm_16652855_x_t4_mirrorless_digital_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) now that the X-T5 is out.

[![Image 33: Fuji X-T3 Image Sample (2)](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/Fuji-X-T3-Image-Sample-2.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/Fuji-X-T3-Image-Sample-2.jpg)

Captured with Fuji X-T4 + XF 23mmF2 R WR @ 23mm, ISO 160, 0.6 sec, f/5.6

### 18. Fujifilm X-H2S

If you want speed in a crop-sensor camera, the [Fuji X-H2S](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1708265-REG/fujifilm_16756924_x_h2s_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) is for you. It has a stacked 26MP sensor, which is plenty of resolution for most situations. And it’s _fast_.

[![Image 34: H2s](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2022/05/H2s.jpg/w=650)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/H2s.jpg)

Thanks to the camera’s stacked BSI sensor, it can shoot RAW photos at 40 FPS. At that frame rate, your buffer is still a very reasonable 140 images. Drop the burst down to 15 FPS, and you’ll get a 1000-image buffer. So, to say that this camera is good for fast action is an understatement.

The X-H2S also has some very impressive video features with excellent-quality footage – not only with 4K120 but also with 6K 30p. Between this camera and the X-T5 above, I consider the X-T5 more versatile because of its higher-resolution sensor, but the X-H2S isn’t far behind.

### 19. Canon EOS R7

Another fast, APS-C camera that has been turning a lot of heads is the Canon EOS R7. [At $1500](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1707911-REG/canon_eos_r7_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1178028/SID/DFF), it’s about $1000 less expensive than the Fuji X-H2S while nipping at its heels in terms of features.

![Image 35: Canon EOS R7 Front](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2022/05/Canon-EOS-R7-Front.jpg/w=650)

Those features begin with a 32.5-megapixel sensor, which is high for an APS-C camera. The EOS R7 has a 30 FPS burst, 4K 60p filming, in-body image stabilization, and a great autofocus system. It also has one of my favorite features, a pre-release burst mode that allows you to record photos up to 1/2 second before you’ve fully pressed the shutter button. This is great for unpredictable wildlife photography.

One potential issue is that the buffer is not as big as that of the Fuji X-H2S. The Canon EOS R7 gives you 93 shots at 30 FPS and 187 shots at 15 FPS (assuming that you’re using lossless compressed CRAW). These figures are not low, but not best-in-class either. Even so,the EOS R7 would be one of my first choices for sports and wildlife photography on a budget today.

### 20. Nikon Z50 II

Nikon’s attempt at a high-speed APS-C camera is the Z50 II, and it’s a very good camera in many ways. The autofocus system is borrowed from the flagship Nikon Z9, so it’s a highly capable camera for sports and wildlife photography.

![Image 36: Nikon Z50 II_01](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_01.jpg/w=650)

The main downside of this camera is the 20 megapixel resolution – tied for the lowest on this list. 20 megapixels is still plenty for most prints, but it doesn’t leave as much room for cropping, and in today’s world, a lot of people would prefer something over 30 MP just in case they’re making large prints.

Still, the price is good ([around $1000](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1860621-REG/nikon_1784_z50_ii_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400)) and the features are very impressive. This camera could be an excellent choice depending on your priorities.

[![Image 37: Nikon Z50 II_Sample Images_DSC_0263](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_Sample-Images_DSC_0263.jpg/w=960)](https://photographylife.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Nikon-Z50-II_Sample-Images_DSC_0263.jpg)

NIKON Z50_2 + NIKKOR Z 180-600mm f/5.6-6.3 VR @ 600mm, ISO 25600, 1/250, f/6.3

### 21. Canon EOS R8

This 24-megapixel, full-frame mirrorless camera is aimed at a budget-conscious audience (at least among full-frame cameras) with a price of $1500. It sometimes goes on sale for less; [check the current price](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1748813-REG/canon_eos_r8_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400/DFF/d10-v21-t1-x1219667/SID/DFF)).

![Image 38: Canon EOS R8 Official Product Photo](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2023/02/Canon-EOS-R8-Official-Product-Photo.jpg/w=650)

Benefits of the EOS R8 include 40 FPS shooting (electronic shutter) and Canon’s pre-release shutter mode. A drawback of this camera is that it doesn’t have in-body image stabilization, and it has just a single SD card slot. Still, these compromises are what allowed Canon to keep the price of the EOS R8 relatively low. It’s still a great camera with impressive bang for your buck.

### 22. OM System OM-1

In the realm of micro four thirds, the [OM System OM-1](https://www.bhphotovideo.com/c/product/1688415-REG/om_system_v210010bu000_om_1_mirrorless_camera.html/BI/5562/KBID/6400) is an amazing camera for sports photography and wildlife photography. It also has some of the most modern features of any camera on this list.

![Image 39: OM1_OM_SYSTEM](https://photographylife.com/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/GrQZt6ZFhE4jsKqjDEtqRA/photographylife.com/2018/12/OM1_OM_SYSTEM.png/w=9999)

Not only does it have a stacked 20MP sensor, it has an insane 120fps burst capability and advanced subject recognition modes for almost every situation.If you don’t want to carry around a massive full-frame camera, and you want access to some very compact, yet high-quality lenses, the OM-1 is worth considering.

The downside, of course, is the smaller sensor size. Obviously Micro Four Thirds has a dedicated audience of photographers, and for something like wildlife or macro photography, it’s may not be a hinderance at all. But bigger sensors allow you to shoot in low-light conditions more easily, and they give you more flexibility in your depth of field. To match a full-frame camera with an 85mm f/1.2 lens, for example, you would need a (nonexistent) 42mm f/0.6 on Micro Four Thirds.

Whether that matters to you or not depends on your style of photography. If you’re not the type to need maximum dynamic range, high ISO performance, or shallow depth of field, the OM-1 can beat almost any other camera on this list in features.The fact that such an amazing camera is low on our list is not a negative for the OM-1, but rather a statement about how good today’s mirrorless cameras are.

### Conclusion

I hope this article helped you get a sense of where things stand as of 2026, from someone who has used literally dozens of mirrorless cameras during my time reviewing them on Photography Life.
